headword: Rock and Roll Hall of Fame
sort_key: rock and roll hall of fame
entry: Music museum and hall of fame in downtown [[Cleveland]], Ohio, on the shore of [[Lake Erie]]. It documents the history of [[Rock music|rock music]] and the artists, producers, engineers and others who influenced its development. The foundation was established on April 20, 1983, by Ahmet Ertegun, founder and chairman of Atlantic Records. After a long search, Cleveland was chosen in 1986 as the permanent home; civic leaders pledged $65 million in public money for construction. Architect [[I. M. Pei]] designed the building, which was dedicated on September 1, 1995.

Genre of popular music, originating in the United States in the late 1940s and early 1950s. It blended African-American styles, mainly [[Rhythm and blues]], with gospel, jazz, boogie-woogie, electric blues, jump blues, swing and folk music. Its early elements appear in blues records of the 1920s and country records of the 1930s, but the genre did not acquire its name until 1954. Piano or saxophone usually led the earliest styles, and the [[Electric guitar|electric guitar]] generally replaced or supplemented them in the mid-to-late 1950s. The beat is a dance rhythm with an accentuated backbeat, usually supplied by a snare drum. By the mid-1960s it had developed into the broader international style of [[Rock music|rock music]]. The music strongly influenced American lifestyles, fashion and language. According to G. C. Altschuler, it had a positive influence on the [[Civil rights movement|civil rights movement]].

Human-made markings placed on natural rock surfaces, typically vertical stone faces. A high proportion of surviving rock art is in [[Cave|caves]] or partly enclosed rock shelters, where it is called cave art or parietal art. Its four main techniques are [[Cave painting|cave paintings]] and petrographs, petroglyphs carved or scratched into the surface, sculpted rock reliefs, and geoglyphs formed on the ground. The oldest known examples date from the Upper Paleolithic and have been found in Europe, Australia, Asia and Africa. Anthropologists believe the works likely had magico-religious significance. [[Indigenous peoples]] often regard rock art as sacred and as part of their cultural heritage, and sites can become significant sources of cultural tourism. The sub-discipline of rock art studies developed in the late 19th century among Francophone scholars studying Upper Paleolithic cave art in Western Europe.

Climbing discipline that involves ascending natural rock outdoors or artificial walls, mostly indoors. Routes range from a few meters to over 1,000 meters (3,300 ft) in height and are documented in guidebooks and online databases. Popular rock types include [[Granite]], [[Limestone]] and sandstone. Contemporary climbing emphasizes free climbing, in which no mechanical aids are used to assist upward movement. Lead climbers use either removable protection, called traditional climbing, or permanently fixed bolts, called sport climbing. The main types trace their origins to late 19th-century Europe, including bouldering in Fontainebleau, big-wall climbing in the [[Dolomites]] and single-pitch climbing in the [[Lake District]] and Saxony. Lead climbing, bouldering and speed climbing became medal events at the Summer Olympics. Debate continues over the use of bolted protection on outdoor routes.

Wild [[Bird|bird]] of the family [[Columbidae]], ancestor of the domestic pigeon. Also called the common pigeon or rock pigeon, it was formally described in 1789 by Johann Friedrich Gmelin, who coined the binomial name *Columba livia*. Wild rock doves are uniformly pale gray with two black bars on each wing, and the sexes show few differences. About [[Breed|1,000 breeds]] of domestic pigeon descend from the species, and escaped domestic birds gave rise to feral pigeons worldwide. Wild birds forage on open and semi-open ground and nest on [[Cliff|cliffs]] and rock ledges. Originating in southern Europe, North Africa and Western Asia, the species is classed by the IUCN as least concern. Estimates put the wild and feral population at 17 to 28 million birds in Europe alone and up to 120 million worldwide.

American industrial, political and banking family. The family owns one of the world's largest fortunes, earned mainly in the American petroleum industry in the late 19th and early 20th centuries by brothers [[John D. Rockefeller]] and William A. Rockefeller Jr., who headed [[Standard Oil]], predecessor of [[ExxonMobil]], [[Saudi Aramco]] and Chevron. The family long controlled Chase Manhattan Bank, and by 1987 it was considered one of the most powerful families in American history. The Rockefellers originated in the Rhineland in Germany and moved to the Americas in the early 18th century.

Non-airbreathing engine used to propel a missile or vehicle. It is a reaction engine that produces thrust by ejecting reaction mass rearward, usually a high-speed jet of hot gas from the [[Combustion|combustion]] of propellant stored inside the rocket. Because it carries its own oxidizer, it can operate in a [[Vacuum|vacuum]], unlike most jet engines. Vehicles propelled by rocket engines include [[Missile|missiles]], artillery shells, ballistic missiles and space vehicles. Compared with other jet engines, rocket engines typically have the highest thrust but the lowest specific impulse, making them the least propellant-efficient, although some types, such as Hall-effect thrusters, are very efficient. Black powder, discovered by ninth-century Chinese alchemists, led to fire arrows, among the first rocket engines to leave the ground. Konstantin Tsiolkovsky first wrote about liquid-fueled rocket engines in the later 19th century.

American professional boxer and world heavyweight champion (1952–56). Raised in Brockton, [[Massachusetts]], he competed from 1947 to 1955 and was known for relentless aggression, punching power and a durable chin. He took the title from Jersey Joe Walcott, and his six title defenses were against Walcott, Roland La Starza, Ezzard Charles (twice), Don Cockell and Archie Moore. He retired undefeated, the only heavyweight champion to do so, and his career knockout-to-win percentage of 87.8% remains one of the highest in heavyweight history.

American sports drama film directed by John G. Avildsen (1976). Written by and starring [[Sylvester Stallone]], it follows Rocky Balboa, a poor small-time club fighter and loan shark debt collector from [[Philadelphia]] who gets a shot at the world heavyweight title held by Apollo Creed. It cost about $1 million to make. It became the highest-grossing film of 1976, earning approximately $225 million worldwide, and received 10 [[Academy Awards|Academy Award]] nominations, winning three, including Best Picture. In 2006 the [[Library of Congress]] selected it for preservation in the United States National Film Registry.

Western style of architecture, art and decoration that emerged in France in the 1730s as a reaction against the Louis XIV style. Characterized by extensive ornamentation, fluid curves, asymmetry and a smaller scale designed to foster intimacy, it often blends white and pastel colors with gilding and uses *rocaille* shell- and pebble-like motifs. Its visual art favors aristocratic leisure and the pastoral. It is regarded as the final expression of the [[Baroque]] movement, and it spread from French interiors to northern Italy, Austria, southern Germany, [[Central Europe]] and Russia, influencing [[Painting|painting]], [[Sculpture|sculpture]], furniture, music, theater and literature. It was later adapted to church architecture, especially in Central Europe, Portugal and [[South America]]. Critics first used the word in print in 1825 as a pejorative, and by the late 18th century the style had largely been replaced by [[Neoclassicism]].

Australian tennis player, world No. 1 among professionals for 1965–69. He won 200 singles titles across his amateur and professional careers, the most of any tennis player, including 11 major singles titles and eight pro majors. He won the [[Grand Slam (tennis)|Grand Slam]] in singles twice, in 1962 and 1969; the latter remains the only time a man has done so in the Open Era. He completed the Pro Slam in 1967 and is the only player in [[Tennis|tennis]] history, male or female, to have won titles on all court surfaces of his time. He also contributed to five Davis Cup titles for Australia. The Rod Laver Arena at the Australian Open and the Laver Cup are named after him.

American screenwriter and television producer, known for live television dramas of the 1950s and the anthology series [[The Twilight Zone]]. He was raised in Binghamton, New York, and was active in politics both on and off the screen. He helped form television industry standards. He was known as the "angry young man" of Hollywood for clashing with executives and sponsors over censorship, racism and war. He was nominated for nine Primetime Emmy Awards, winning six.

British singer and songwriter with a distinctive raspy voice. He began busking in 1962, joined the [[Jeff Beck]] Group in 1967 and launched a solo career in 1969. His breakthrough album, *Every Picture Tells a Story* (1971), included the hit "Maggie May". The disco-tinged hit "Da Ya Think I'm Sexy?" topped the charts in the United States and United Kingdom. Stewart has sold more than 120 million records worldwide. He was inducted into the [[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame]] in 1994 and again as a member of Faces in 2012.

American actor born in [[London]], active on stage and screen for six decades. He was a child star in England before his mother took him to the United States after the outbreak of [[World War II]]. His American film career began with *Man Hunt* (1941), directed by [[Fritz Lang]], followed by *How Green Was My Valley* (1941) and *Lassie Come Home* (1943). He won a Tony Award for Jean Anouilh's *The Fighting Cock* and played Mordred in the Broadway musical *Camelot*. He played the chimpanzees Cornelius and Caesar in the *Planet of the Apes* films (1968–73).

Canadian [[Professional wrestling|professional wrestler]] and actor. Billed as coming from Glasgow, Scotland, he was known for his kilt and [[Bagpipes|bagpipe]] entrance music, which referenced his Scottish heritage. He wrestled mainly for the [[WWE|World Wrestling Federation]] and World Championship Wrestling between 1984 and 2000, and headlined WrestleMania and Starrcade. He accumulated 34 championships and hosted the interview segment "Piper's Pit". The Daily Telegraph described him as "considered by many to be the greatest 'heel' (or villain) wrestler ever." He was inducted into the WWE Hall of Fame in 2005. His film roles include the lead in *They Live* (1988).

Competitive equestrian sport arising from the working practices of [[Cattle|cattle]] herding in Spain and Mexico. It was originally based on the skills of working vaqueros and later cowboys in the western United States, western Canada and northern Mexico. Professional events include tie-down roping, team roping, steer wrestling, saddle bronc riding, bareback bronc riding, bull riding, breakaway roping and barrel racing. The "world's first public cowboy contest" was held on July 4, 1883, in Pecos, [[Texas]]. Rodeo is the official state sport of [[Wyoming]], Montana, South Dakota and Texas. The professional season ends with the National Finals Rodeo in Las Vegas each December. [[Animal rights|Animal rights]] advocates argue that some competitions constitute animal cruelty, and some local and state governments have restricted rodeos. Rodeo is banned in the [[United Kingdom]] and the Netherlands.

American songwriting team of composer Richard Rodgers and lyricist-dramatist Oscar Hammerstein II. Their first collaboration, *Oklahoma!* (1943), integrated song and dance into the plot and helped launch the "golden age" of musical theater. Five of their Broadway shows, *Oklahoma!*, *Carousel*, *South Pacific*, *The King and I* and *The Sound of Music*, were outstanding successes, as was the television broadcast of [[Cinderella]] (1957). Their works earned 34 Tony Awards, 15 [[Academy Awards|Academy Awards]], two [[Pulitzer Prize|Pulitzer Prizes]] and two [[Grammy Awards|Grammy Awards]]. Their partnership has been called the greatest of the 20th century.

[[Supercontinent]] of the [[Proterozoic|Mesoproterozoic and Neoproterozoic]] eras. It assembled 1.26–0.90 billion years ago and broke up 750–633 million years ago. Reconstructions of its layout differ in many details, and paleomagnetic data constrain latitude far better than longitude. The name, from the Russian for "motherland," was given in 1990. Its fragments reassembled into Pannotia 633–573 million years ago. Extreme cooling around 717–635 million years ago, the [[Snowball Earth]] of the Cryogenian period, and rapid evolution of life in the [[Ediacaran]] and [[Cambrian]] periods may have been triggered by the breakup or by slowed tectonic activity.

American stand-up comedian, actor and screenwriter. Known for self-deprecating one-liners and the catchphrase "I don’t get no respect!", he began at the Fantasy Lounge in New York City and became a headliner on the [[Las Vegas]] casino circuit. His breakout role as a boorish golfer in *Caddyshack* (1980) led to comedies including *Easy Money* (1983) and *Back to School* (1986). He played an abusive father in [[Oliver Stone]]'s *Natural Born Killers* (1994). His album *No Respect* (1980) won the Grammy Award for Best Comedy Album. He died after a month in a [[Coma|coma]] caused by complications from heart valve surgery.

African-American man whose beating by [[Los Angeles]] police officers became a symbol of police brutality. On March 3, 1991, he was severely beaten during an arrest after a high-speed pursuit on [[California]] freeways. A bystander's video of the beating was broadcast worldwide. Three of the four officers were charged with excessive force, and their acquittal in 1992 sparked the [[1992 Los Angeles riots]]. King appeared on television to plead for peace, a plea often paraphrased as "Can we all just get along?" In a 1994 civil suit, King won $3.8 million from the city.

Small, reddish and gray-brown [[Deer|deer]] widespread from the Mediterranean to [[Scandinavia]]. Its range extends from Scotland to the [[Caucasus]] and east into northern Iran. The male is called a roebuck, and the English name derives from [[Old English]] rā. Linnaeus first described it in 1758 as *Cervus capreolus*. The species is well adapted to cold environments. Populations grow somewhat larger eastward, peaking in Kazakhstan, and the eastern populations were later recognized as a separate species, the eastern or Siberian roe deer.

Landmark 1973 decision of the U.S. Supreme Court on [[Abortion|abortion]]. The Court ruled that the [[Constitution of the United States|Constitution]] protected a pregnant woman's right to choose an abortion before fetal viability. The case was brought by Norma McCorvey, known as "Jane Roe," who lived in [[Texas]], where abortion was legal only to save the mother's life. In a 7–2 decision the Court found a "right to privacy" under the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment, but it balanced that right against state interests and set a trimester framework for regulation. The decision was overruled in 2022 in *Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health Organization*.

American film critic, historian and author. He wrote for the *Chicago Sun-Times* from 1967 until his death and in 1975 became the first film critic to win the Pulitzer Prize for Criticism. With Gene Siskel, he co-hosted the [[PBS|PBS]] program *Sneak Previews* and later *At the Movies*, helping popularize nationally televised film reviewing. They trademarked the phrase "Two Thumbs Up." He championed [[Werner Herzog]], Errol Morris, [[Spike Lee]] and [[Martin Scorsese]]. Diagnosed with cancer in 2002, he later lost part of his jaw and could no longer speak or eat normally, but kept writing until his death.

Swiss former professional [[Tennis|tennis]] player. He was ranked world No. 1 in men's singles for 310 weeks, including a record 237 consecutive weeks, and won 103 singles titles on the ATP Tour. His 20 major singles titles included a men's record eight at Wimbledon and a joint Open Era record five at the US Open, and he completed the [[Grand Slam (tennis)|career Grand Slam]] at the 2009 French Open. He was one of the "Big Three" with [[Rafael Nadal]] and [[Novak Djokovic]], who dominated men's tennis for nearly two decades. Federer won Olympic doubles gold in 2008 and led Switzerland to its first Davis Cup title in 2014. He retired in September 2022. He founded the Roger Federer Foundation, which supports impoverished children in southern Africa.

Norman king of [[Sicily]] (1130–1154), known as Roger the Great. He inherited the County of Sicily in 1105, under the regency of his mother, Adelaide del Vasto, after the death of his brother Simon. He became duke of [[Calabria|Apulia and Calabria]] in 1127, and Pope Honorius II, who had opposed the union of Sicily and Apulia, invested him as duke at Benevento in 1128. He was crowned king of Sicily in 1130 and became king of Africa in 1148. At his court in [[Palermo]], the geographer Muhammad al-Idrisi produced the *Tabula Rogeriana*.
